Chapter 10: Toward a More Merciful Future — Lessons and Possibilities
Over the years, as more and more cases came across my desk, I just couldn’t ignore the patterns anymore. The cracks in the system were everywhere—sometimes plain as day, sometimes hidden just beneath the surface. But you know what? Even with all its flaws, the system wasn’t beyond hope. Things could change, if only people were willing to imagine something better.
Take the story of a judge I once knew. He started to question the very sentences he was handing down. Instead of keeping his distance, he began visiting the prisons, meeting the people whose lives he’d altered, and really listening to what they had to say. Those conversations changed him in ways he couldn’t have predicted. He became a champion for second chances, pushing for programs that focused on rehabilitation instead of just punishment. Sure, his colleagues raised their eyebrows. But he kept going, believing with all his heart that true mercy isn’t a weakness—it’s a sign of real wisdom.
There were lawmakers, too—folks who’d heard story after story about the impact of harsh sentencing laws. They decided enough was enough. Even when faced with loud opposition from those clinging to “tough on crime” policies, they kept fighting. Over time, they managed to pass laws that cut down on mandatory minimums, opened up access to mental health care, and gave people a shot at redemption.
Here’s something most people overlook: each of us has the power to shape what comes next. The system isn’t some faceless machine. It’s made up of real people—judges, lawyers, lawmakers, voters—and every single one plays a part. When enough people raise their voices for change, the system has to listen.
What became crystal clear was that mercy isn’t just a private virtue—it’s something we need in public life, too. A truly just society recognizes the humanity in everyone, even those who’ve stumbled or made mistakes. It’s a place that believes in redemption, that people can grow, and that compassion can be the most powerful force for good.
The stories of those who’ve worked for a more merciful future remind us: justice isn’t some finish line you cross. It’s a journey. And walking that path takes courage, empathy, and a real willingness to see the world through someone else’s eyes.
